result: Screening of 70 SIVmac239-infected macaques identified 9 NAb-inducing animals, 7 of which selected for a specific CD8+ T-cell escape mutation (Nef-G63E) in viral nef before NAb induction. NAb inducers showed persistent viremia comparable to non-inducers, with average maximum NAb titers of 1:16 induced at ~48 weeks post-infection. The Nef-G63E mutation was significantly enriched in NAb inducers compared to non-inducers and preceded or paralleled NAb induction.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C35-C36, C43-C48, C51-C52, C56-C58 provide converging evidence from screening data, viral load measurements, NAb titer quantification, and temporal sequencing analysis. The statistical enrichment of Nef-G63E in NAb inducers (C57) and temporal precedence (C58) are supported by data in Figures 1-2. Sample sizes are adequate (n=70 screened, n=9 NAb inducers, n=19 controls), and statistical tests are appropriately applied.

result: The Nef-G63E mutation is a CD8+ T-cell escape mutation from Nef62-70 QW9-specific responses restricted by MHC-I alleles Mamu-B*004:01, Mamu-B*039:01, or Mamu-A1*032:02. Seven NAb inducers selecting Nef-G63E elicited CD8+ T-cell responses to this epitope. While 10/19 NAb non-inducers possessed these MHC-I alleles, NAb induction required specific selection of the Nef-G63E mutation, not just MHC-I genotype possession.
evaluation: Claims C59-C68 are well-supported by CD8+ T-cell response data (Figure 3A-B), MHC-I genotyping, and statistical analysis (p=0.25 for MHC-I allele distribution, C64). The distinction between MHC-I possession and mutation selection (C65) is appropriately demonstrated. The escape mutation confirmation (C66) and CD8+ T-cell dependence (C68) are supported by functional assays.

result: The Nef-G63E mutation does not critically impair viral replication or alter canonical Nef functions. In vitro replication was comparable to WT on HSC-F cells, plasma viral loads were similar between Nef-G63E-selecting NAb inducers and non-inducers, and the mutation did not affect downregulation of CD3, CD4, MHC-I, CXCR4, or BST-2. Plasma ferritin levels showed no differences between groups.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by in vitro replication assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), in vivo viral load comparisons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), surface molecule downregulation assays (Figure 4A), and ferritin measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). These data effectively rule out replication defects and canonical Nef function changes as explanations for NAb induction.

result: The Nef-G63E mutation significantly reduces pAkt Ser473 phosphorylation in infected cells compared to WT, with a more pronounced effect than in PI3K gain-of-function APDS mice. The pAkt Thr308 level remained unaffected. This Akt-inhibitory phenotype is PI3K stimuli-dependent, with accelerated appearance under serum starvation, cytokine stimulation, or high-MOI infection. Transcriptome analysis showed decreased PI3K-pAkt-FoxO1-related gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C75-C82 are strongly supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4B-C), transcriptome analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and multiple experimental conditions. The comparison to APDS mice (C76) provides important context. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p=0.0009, C75), and the PI3K stimuli-dependence (C81) is validated through multiple approaches. The specificity for Ser473 vs. Thr308 (C77) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation.

result: The Nef-G63E mutation causes significant decreases in Nef binding to PI3K p85/p110α and mTORC2 components (mTOR, GβL/mLST8, Sin1) in infected cells. This attenuates PI3K/mTORC2 signaling driven by aberrant Nef bridging, explaining decreased Akt Ser473 phosphorylation. Nef-G63E SIV infection results in more pronounced apoptosis of infected cells, manifesting a molecular signature reciprocal to human APDS.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by proximity ligation assay (Figure 4D), coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 4E), and cell death assays (Figure 4F). The mechanistic link between decreased binding, reduced Akt phosphorylation, and increased apoptosis is logically coherent. Statistical significance is demonstrated for all binding partners (p<0.05). The reciprocal APDS comparison (C93) is well-justified by the molecular data.

result: Lymph node Env-specific B cells showed significantly higher Nef-positive frequencies compared to non-Env-specific B cells, indicating preferential targeting by infected cell-derived Nef. Nef invasion upregulated pAkt Ser473 in Nef-invaded B cells in vivo to levels resembling in vitro analysis, demonstrating that Nef-driven aberrant PI3K/mTORC2 signaling occurs in Nef-invaded B cells in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 are supported by sophisticated imaging cytometry with machine learning-based noise cancellation (Figure 5). The preferential targeting of Env-specific B cells (C97) is statistically significant (p=0.015, Figure 5D). The pAkt upregulation in vivo (C100-C101) validates the mechanistic model. The technical approach addresses potential artifacts through triple noise cancellation, strengthening confidence in the findings.

result: In vitro coculture experiments demonstrated that CD3 stimulation enhanced adhesion of Nef+ T cells to B cells and increased Nef acquisition by B cells. Polarized Nef protrusion/injection from T cells to B cells and trogocytosed B-cell membranes were detected. Coculture with primary CD20+ B cells recapitulated decreased pAkt Ser473 phosphorylation upon G63E Nef transfer compared to WT Nef, indicating the mutation can directly alleviate maturation inhibition in Nef-targeted B cells.
evaluation: Claims C102-C109 are supported by imaging flow cytometry (Figure 6A), conventional flow cytometry (Figure 6B), and primary B-cell coculture experiments (Figure 6C). The contact-dependent mechanism is well-demonstrated through multiple approaches. Statistical significance is shown (p=0.027 for CD3 enhancement, p=0.0018 for pAkt reduction). The in vitro recapitulation of the in vivo phenotype (C108-C109) strengthens the mechanistic model.

result: NAb inducers showed significantly higher Env-specific IgG+ plasmablast responses around week 30 post-infection after Nef-G63E selection compared to non-inducers. Two-dimensional vector analysis of Env-specific memory B cells and plasmablasts revealed that NAb non-inducers converged on an attractor area (Dn) representing failed GC output, while NAb inducers tracked outside Dn and converged on a distinct attractor area (Di) at NAb induction, indicating more robust virus-specific B-cell responses.
evaluation: Claims C110-C116 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 7B-C) and novel two-dimensional vector analysis (Figure 7D). Statistical significance is demonstrated (Mann-Whitney U tests, p<0.0001 for attractor area exclusivity). The temporal relationship between Nef-G63E selection and enhanced B-cell responses is well-established. The comparison to APDS (C116) is appropriately cited. The vector analysis provides a creative approach to visualizing GC output dynamics.

result: Another CTL escape mutant, Nef-G63R, was selected with marginal statistical significance primarily in early stage but did not associate with NAb induction even upon preferential selection in one animal. Nef-G63R was not similarly decreased in pAkt drive compared to Nef-G63E, indicating that the Nef-G63E mutation was more tightly linked with NAb induction in terms of immunosignaling phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by mutation frequency analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B) and pAkt measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C). This negative control strengthens the specificity of the Nef-G63E-NAb association. The comparison demonstrates that not all CTL escape mutations in this region produce the NAb-inducing phenotype, supporting the mechanistic specificity of the G63E mutation.

result: In SIVmac239-infected macaques, Nef62-70-specific CD8+ T-cell responses selected for the Nef-G63E escape mutant, which displays attenuated Nef binding and drive of B-cell-inhibitory PI3K/mTORC2. Nef invasion preferentially targeted Env-specific B cells in vivo. These events predisposed to enhanced Env-specific B-cell responses and NAb induction in a manner reciprocal to human APDS-mediated immune dysregulation, demonstrating how NAb responses can be shaped by both cellular and humoral adaptive immune pressure.
evaluation: Claims C117-C122, C166-C167 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The integration of CD8+ T-cell escape, altered Nef-PI3K/mTORC2 signaling, preferential B-cell targeting, and enhanced B-cell responses is well-supported by the collective data. The reciprocal APDS comparison is justified by the magnitude of pAkt changes (C76, C122). This represents a novel mechanism linking cellular and humoral immunity in lentiviral infection.

result: The study demonstrates that the Nef-G63E mutation reduces excess Nef interaction-mediated drive of B-cell maturation-limiting PI3K/mTORC2, with preferential Nef perturbation of Env-specific B cells suggesting polarized contact-dependent transfer. This pattern is extrinsically reciprocal to human PI3K gain-of-function antibody-dysregulating disease (APDS). The findings indicate that harnessing the PI3K/mTORC2 axis may facilitate NAb induction against difficult-to-neutralize viruses including HIV/SIV.
evaluation: While claims C6-C11, C37, C40-C42, C93, C121, C145-C146, C150, C168 are supported by the experimental data showing the reciprocal relationship to APDS, the translational claim that 'harnessing the PI3K/mTORC2 axis may facilitate NAb induction' (C11, C42, C168) is speculative. No manipulation experiments targeting PI3K/mTORC2 were performed to test this hypothesis. The authors acknowledge this limitation (C165) and note that 'manipulation/reconstitution experiments shall be designed.' The mechanistic understanding is solid, but therapeutic application requires additional validation.

result: NAb inducers and non-inducers showed similar patterns of viral env sequence variations, mainly in V1, V2, and V4 regions. SIV antigen-specific binding antibody responses were rather decreased in NAb inducers, with lower Env-binding IgG titers at year 1 post-infection compared to non-inducers, consistent with other reports and differing from Nef-deleted SIV infection.
evaluation: Claims C50, C94, C48-C49 are supported by env sequencing data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and Env-binding IgG measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C). The observation that NAb inducers have lower binding antibody titers is counterintuitive but well-documented and consistent with prior literature (C49). This suggests quality over quantity in the B-cell response and supports the maturation-focused mechanism proposed.

result: The Nef-G63E mutation may be T helper cell cytopathic and decrease Th dysfunctional expansion. Reduced chronic-phase peripheral memory Tfh was somewhat consistent with this notion. The interval between Nef-G63E selection and NAb induction was variable and may be influenced by basal competitive balance between humoral and cellular adaptive immunity. The influence of the Nef-G63E phenotype on CD4+ T cells in vivo and its consequence on B-cell modulation remains largely elusive.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C129-C130, C159-C161 address Tfh responses and the variable timing of NAb induction. While reduced Tfh is observed (C84, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F), the mechanistic link to the Nef-G63E phenotype is speculative (C83). The variable interval between mutation selection and NAb induction (C129) is acknowledged but not explained. The authors appropriately note that 'influence of the Nef-G63E phenotype on CD4+ T cells in vivo...remains largely elusive' (C159). Further studies are needed (C161).

result: This work is the first to interlink a PI3K/mTORC2-modulating viral signature and enhanced B-cell/NAb responses in a viral infection model, evidencing a new pattern of NAb responses bivalently shaped through viral interactions with both humoral and cellular immunity. The current Nef-G63E phenotype adds another aspect to the multifaceted impact of Nef in HIV/SIV infection, differing from Nef-deleted viruses. The SIV Nef N-terminal region is not conserved in HIV-1, and whether similar phenotypes exist in HIV-1 remains to be addressed.
evaluation: Claims C123, C127, C131-C135 appropriately contextualize the novelty and limitations of the findings. The claim of being 'first to interlink' (C123) appears justified based on the literature review. The distinction from Nef-deleted viruses (C132) is well-supported by data and citations. The acknowledgment of limited HIV-1 conservation (C133-C134) and suggestions for future work (C135) are appropriate. The novelty claim is supported by the unique mechanistic insights.

result: Study limitations include the use of retrospective samples, constraints in optimally timing lymph node cell sampling, unavailability of certain plasma and cellular samples in different experiments, and incomplete investigation of the observed polarity of Env-specific B-cell perturbation in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C155-C158 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The retrospective nature (C155) does constrain temporal resolution of B-cell perturbation dynamics. Sample availability issues (C156-C157) are transparently reported and explain some data gaps. The acknowledgment that 'much remains to be investigated' for B-cell perturbation polarity (C158) is appropriate given the complexity of the in vivo system. These limitations do not invalidate the major findings but indicate areas for future prospective studies.

result: Background claims establish that HIV/SIV infections impair NAb responses through B-cell/antibody-inhibitory countermeasures, that sequential virus-host B-cell interaction is required for NAb induction, and that driver molecular signatures remain largely unknown. Various NAb induction signatures have been reported, indicating redundant pathways. SIVmac239 is a difficult-to-neutralize, pathogenic strain in macaques that generally lacks NAb responses, making it an attractive model to analyze NAb induction mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C34 provide well-established background supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims appropriately set up the knowledge gap (C3, C21, C30) and rationale for the study (C26-C27, C32). The characterization of SIVmac239 (C33-C34) is well-documented. These background claims are appropriately cited and provide necessary context for the experimental work.

result: Preferential Nef transfer to Env-specific B cells suggests polarized perturbation in cognate immune cells in vivo, potentially involving hijacking of cognate T-cell/B-cell interactions. Enhanced T-cell attachment and Nef transfer by TCR stimulation may override infection-mediated cytoskeletal impairment. Tfh cells bearing trogocytosed CD20 and positive for viral DNA appear during SIV infection, consistent with contact-dependent, polarized interactions facilitating Nef transfer to cognate B cells.
evaluation: Claims C136-C141 integrate the current findings with prior observations about polarized immune interactions. The preferential targeting (C136) is supported by Figure 5D. The speculation about hijacking cognate interactions (C138) is reasonable given the MHC class II context (C137). The TCR stimulation effects (C139) are supported by Figure 6. The citation of Tfh trogocytosis (C140-C141) provides independent corroboration. While some elements are speculative, they are appropriately qualified and supported by the data.

result: The study measures autologous neutralization of SIVmac239, which differs from HIV-specific broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs). However, signatures of enhanced IgG+ Env-specific antibody-forming cells and B cells (class switch/terminal differentiation) and virus neutralization (hypermutation) indicate elevated activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) activity, suggesting strong conceptual continuity with bNAb regulation by AID in HIV infection.
evaluation: Claims C142-C144 appropriately clarify the scope of the study while connecting to broader bNAb biology. The distinction between autologous neutralization and bNAbs (C142) is important and clearly stated. The inference about AID activity (C143) is reasonable given the observed B-cell phenotypes (class switching, hypermutation). The claim of 'strong conceptual continuity' (C144) is justified, as AID is indeed central to both autologous NAb and bNAb development. This contextualization strengthens the translational relevance.

result: APDS occurs from germline mutations in PIK3CD or PIK3R1, causing class IA PI3K gain of function that interferes with cognate B cells, leading to impaired B-cell class switching. The exact hierarchy of Nef binding to PI3K/mTORC2 components remains to be investigated, though PI3Kp85 showed the strongest Nef-binding. Decreased Nef-PI3Kp85 binding may precipitate into attenuated interactions with PI3K/mTORC2, similar to domino-triggering in APDS patients. Gain-of-function mutations in PI3K-encoding genes affect B cells more strongly but also evoke dysregulation in CD4+ T cells.
evaluation: Claims C147-C149, C151-C154, C162-C163 provide important context about APDS and PI3K signaling. The APDS background (C147-C149) is well-cited. The acknowledgment that binding hierarchy 'remains to be investigated' (C151) is appropriate. The PI3Kp85 binding data (C152, Figure 4D) and mechanistic speculation (C153) are reasonable. The comparison to APDS domino-triggering (C154) is well-cited. The note about T-cell effects (C162-C163) appropriately acknowledges complexity beyond B cells.

result: Specific animal models like this one help depict temporal cascades of in vivo events leading to NAb induction. As an extension, manipulation/reconstitution experiments shall be designed. Searching for analogies between viral immune dysregulations and human inborn errors of immunity may fuel discovery of novel targets to modulate immune responses in translational settings.
evaluation: Claims C164-C165, C169 appropriately discuss the utility of the model and future directions. The value of the animal model (C164) is demonstrated by the temporal resolution achieved. The call for manipulation experiments (C165) acknowledges the need for causal validation. The broader vision of leveraging IEI-viral dysregulation analogies (C169) is appropriately speculative and well-cited. These forward-looking statements are reasonable given the findings.
